headline: Silicon Quantum Computing and Schneider Electric say a quantum chip improved next-day home energy forecasts by about 20 percent on average in a trial, and the Australian government is now funding a larger test.
score_reason: Pool score 5 lowered by 1 because the headline says 'deploy' but this is a trial, and the accuracy figures come from the companies themselves.
importance_line: Better home energy forecasts could help manage rooftop solar and batteries, but the 20 percent figure is the partners' own, was measured against one comparison method, and the larger test with hundreds of homes has yet to show it holds up.
summary: Interesting Engineering reports that Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) and Schneider Electric, working with UNSW Sydney, say SQC's quantum-enhanced Watermelon chip made next-day energy forecasts about 20 percent more accurate on average, and up to 41 percent in the best case, than a standard computer method, using 12 months of data. The Australian government is giving A$3.6 million (about US$2.5 million) for a second stage covering hundreds of homes, which will test whether the gains hold up beyond the first trial.
notes: Original outlet Computer Weekly (blog) was blocked (403 Cloudflare), so this entry is written from Interesting Engineering; The Quantum Insider's copy of the press release was also read.
